```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)
library(plotly)
set.seed(6400)
options(scipen = 999)

# A known population: right-skewed household incomes (lognormal).
# Because we invent it, we know the TRUE mean exactly — the thing a real
# analyst never gets to see, and the whole point of the demonstration.
meanlog <- 10.8; sdlog <- 0.5
true_mean <- exp(meanlog + sdlog^2 / 2)

boot_mean <- function(x, B) replicate(B, mean(sample(x, length(x), replace = TRUE)))
```

# The question

A survey reports an average, attaches a "95% confidence interval," and moves on.
But what does that phrase actually promise? It is tempting to read it as "there's a
95% chance the true average is in this range" — which is not quite what it means.
This post uses simulation to show what it *does* mean, and then uses the same idea
to explain how a hypothesis test, a p-value, and a "rejection region" work. One
example runs through all of it: estimating the average household income in a town
from a single sample of 50 households.

# Where a confidence interval comes from: the bootstrap

We have one sample of 50 incomes. We want the average, but a single number hides how
much it would wobble if we had drawn a *different* 50 households. The **bootstrap**
estimates that wobble using only the sample we have: draw a new sample of 50 *from
our own sample, with replacement*, take its mean, and repeat thousands of times. The
spread of those bootstrap means approximates the spread of the real sampling
distribution.

```{r}
#| label: fig-bootstrap
#| column: page

big <- rlnorm(250, meanlog, sdlog)      # the data we could collect, in order
ns  <- c(10, 25, 50, 100, 250)

boot_df <- bind_rows(lapply(ns, function(nn) {
  tibble(n = nn, boot_mean = boot_mean(big[1:nn], 2000))
}))

plot_ly(boot_df, x = ~boot_mean, frame = ~n, type = "histogram",
        marker = list(color = "#2c7fb8", line = list(color = "white", width = 0.3))) |>
  layout(
    title = list(text = "Bootstrap distribution of the mean (drag the slider to add data)"),
    xaxis = list(title = "Bootstrap sample mean", tickprefix = "$", range = c(30000, 95000)),
    yaxis = list(title = "Count"),
    shapes = list(list(type = "line", x0 = true_mean, x1 = true_mean,
                       y0 = 0, y1 = 1, yref = "paper",
                       line = list(color = "grey", dash = "dash")))
  ) |>
  animation_opts(frame = 1000, transition = 300, redraw = FALSE) |>
  animation_slider(currentvalue = list(prefix = "Sample size n = "))
```

```{r}
#| label: ci-stats
#| include: false
samp   <- big[1:50]
bm50   <- boot_mean(samp, 5000)
ci     <- quantile(bm50, c(0.025, 0.975))
```

The dashed line marks the true average, `r dollar(true_mean)` — which in real life you
would never know. Drag the slider: with `n = 10` the bootstrap distribution is wide
and the estimate is shaky; by `n = 250` it is tight and centered near the truth. More
data does not change the method, only the *width* of what it produces. From our
50-household sample, the middle 95% of bootstrap means runs from
**`r dollar(ci[1])`** to **`r dollar(ci[2])`** — that interval is our 95% confidence
interval for the average.

# What "95%" is really a statement about

Here is the subtlety. The 95% does not describe *our one* interval; it describes the
*procedure*. If we repeated the whole exercise — draw 50 households, build a 95%
interval — over and over, about 95% of those intervals would contain the true
average, and some would miss. We can just do that.

```{r}
#| label: fig-coverage
#| fig-cap: "Each horizontal line is a 95% confidence interval from a fresh sample of 50. Blue intervals contain the true average (vertical line); red ones miss. Across many repeats, close to 95% catch the truth."
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 5

M <- 200
cis <- t(replicate(M, {
  s  <- rlnorm(50, meanlog, sdlog)
  bm <- boot_mean(s, 1200)
  quantile(bm, c(0.025, 0.975))
}))
cov_df <- tibble(id = 1:M, lo = cis[, 1], hi = cis[, 2],
                 covers = lo <= true_mean & hi >= true_mean)
coverage <- mean(cov_df$covers)

cov_df |>
  arrange((lo + hi) / 2) |>
  mutate(rank = row_number()) |>
  ggplot(aes(y = rank, color = covers)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = lo, xend = hi, yend = rank), linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = true_mean, color = "grey30") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "#2c7fb8", `FALSE` = "#c0392b"),
                     labels = c(`TRUE` = "contains truth", `FALSE` = "misses"), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_dollar()) +
  labs(x = "95% confidence interval", y = "Sample (sorted)",
       title = "Most intervals catch the true mean — but not all") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
```

Out of `r M` intervals, **`r percent(coverage, accuracy = 1)`** contained the true
average. That is what "95% confident" means: not a probability about the one interval
in front of you, but the long-run hit rate of the recipe that made it. Any single
interval either contains the truth or does not; the guarantee is about the method.

# From intervals to tests: simulating the null

The same resampling idea powers a hypothesis test. Suppose a report claims the town's
average income is **`r dollar(65000)`**. Our sample averages well below that — but
could that gap be chance? A test answers by asking: *if the claim were true, how often
would random sampling produce a gap at least as large as the one we saw?*

To simulate that world, we shift our sample so its mean equals the claimed
`r dollar(65000)` — imposing the null hypothesis — then bootstrap it to build the
distribution of sample means we'd expect *if the claim held*.

```{r}
#| label: fig-nulltest
#| fig-cap: "The distribution of the sample mean if the claim ($65,000) were true. Our actual sample mean (black line) sits far out in the tail; the shaded area beyond it — in both directions — is the p-value. The red cut-offs mark the 5% rejection region."
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 4.5

mu0     <- 65000
obs     <- mean(samp)
shifted <- samp - obs + mu0                 # impose the null: mean now = mu0
null_means <- boot_mean(shifted, 5000)

gap     <- abs(obs - mu0)
pval    <- mean(abs(null_means - mu0) >= gap)
cutoffs <- quantile(null_means, c(0.025, 0.975))
verdict <- if (pval < 0.05) "reject" else "fail to reject"

tibble(null_mean = null_means) |>
  mutate(extreme = abs(null_mean - mu0) >= gap) |>
  ggplot(aes(null_mean, fill = extreme)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, color = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = obs, linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = cutoffs, color = "#c0392b", linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = obs, y = Inf, label = "  observed mean", hjust = 0, vjust = 2, size = 3.5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "grey75", `TRUE` = "#2c7fb8"),
                    labels = c(`FALSE` = "typical if claim true", `TRUE` = "as extreme (p-value)"),
                    name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_dollar()) +
  labs(x = "Sample mean if the claim were true", y = "Count",
       title = "Is the gap real, or just chance?") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

The observed mean (`r dollar(obs)`) lands far out in the tail of the "if the claim were
true" distribution. The shaded tail area — the share of simulated means at least as far
from `r dollar(65000)` as ours — is the **p-value**, here **`r round(pval, 3)`**. The
red lines are the **rejection region**: the outer 5% where a result is so unlikely under
the claim that we stop believing the claim. Since the p-value is `r if (pval < 0.05) "below" else "above"`
0.05, we **`r verdict`** the claim at the 5% level.

# Takeaway

Three ideas, one engine. Resampling our own data builds a confidence interval;
repeating the experiment shows that "95%" is the hit rate of the *procedure*, not a
fact about one interval; and resampling under an assumed claim turns a p-value into
something you can see — a shaded tail, not a formula. Simulation does not replace the
mathematics of inference, but it makes the mathematics legible: every abstract term
here is just a picture of repeated sampling.

One honest limit: the bootstrap leans on the sample being representative of the
population, and for very small samples or very skewed data its intervals can run a
little narrow — which is exactly why the coverage check above is worth running rather
than assumed.

---

*This is a self-contained demonstration: the population and every sample are simulated
in the code above with a fixed random seed, so all numbers and figures reproduce
exactly, with no external data. The interactive figure is built with `plotly`; the
rest use `ggplot2`.*
